long_notes.Definition of Relation and its Types:
Definition of Relation

A relation $R$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is a subset of the Cartesian product $A imes B$. Formally, $R\subseteq A imes B$ and an ordered pair $(a,b)\in R$ is read as "$a$ is related to $b$" and denoted $a\,R\,b$.

Notation and basic properties

  • Domain of $R$: $\operatorname{Dom}(R)=\{a\in A\mid \exists b\in B,(a,b)\in R\}$.
  • Range of $R$: $\operatorname{Ran}(R)=\{b\in B\mid \exists a\in A,(a,b)\in R\}$.
  • Inverse relation: $R^{-1}=\{(b,a)\mid (a,b)\in R\}$.

Types of Relations (on a single set $S$)

TypeDefinition
Reflexive$ orall x\in S,(x,x)\in R$
Irreflexive$ orall x\in S,(x,x) otin R$
Symmetric$ orall x,y\in S,(x,y)\in R\Rightarrow (y,x)\in R$
Antisymmetric$ orall x,y\in S,(x,y)\in R\land (y,x)\in R\Rightarrow x=y$
Transitive$ orall x,y,z\in S,(x,y)\in R\land (y,z)\in R\Rightarrow (x,z)\in R$

Edge Cases

  • Empty relation: $R=\emptyset$. It is vacuously symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive but never reflexive.
  • Universal relation: $R=S imes S$. It is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, but not antisymmetric unless $|S|=1$.

Relation as a Function

A relation $f\subseteq A imes B$ is a function if:

  • Every $a\in A$ appears in at least one ordered pair (totality).
  • No $a\in A$ appears in more than one ordered pair (uniqueness).

These two conditions are often written as:

$$ orall a\in A,\ \exists!\,b\in B ext{ such that }(a,b)\in f.$$

Solved Example

Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{a,b\}$. Define $R=\{(1,a),(2,b)\}$.

  1. Find $\operatorname{Dom}(R)$ and $\operatorname{Ran}(R)$.
    $\operatorname{Dom}(R)=\{1,2\}$, $\operatorname{Ran}(R)=\{a,b\}$.
  2. Is $R$ a function from $A$ o $B$?
    The element $3\in A$ does ot appear \in any ordered pair, violating totality. Hence $R$ is ot a function.
  3. Is $R$ symmetric?
    Since $(1,a)\in R$ but $(a,1) otin A imes B$, symmetry is ot applicable for relations between different sets; however, if we view $R$ as a relation on $A\cup B$, symmetry fails because the converse pairs are missing.

Key Takeaway

Understanding a relation as a subset of a Cartesian product provides a unified language for describing mappings, orderings, and equivalence structures. Mastery of the five fundamental properties—reflexivity, irreflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry, and transitivity—enables quick classification of any relation, a skill frequently tested in CBSE Class 12 examinations.
long_notes.Representation of Relations (ordered pai:
Definition (Relation): A relation $R$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is a subset of the Cartesian product $A\times B$. It is written as $R\subseteq A\times B$ and consists of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ where $a\in A$ and $b\in B$.

Representations of a relation:

  • Ordered pairs: List all elements of $R$ explicitly as $(a,b)$.
  • Matrix (or Boolean matrix): Choose a fixed ordering of the elements of $A$ (rows) and $B$ (columns). The matrix $M_R$ is defined by
    $$M_R[i,j]=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }(a_i,b_j)\in R\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
  • Digraph (directed graph): Draw a vertex for every element of $A\cup B$. For each $(a,b)\in R$ draw a directed edge (arrow) from vertex $a$ \to vertex $b$.

Construction of the matrix – step by step:

  1. List the elements of $A$ \in a chosen order $a_1,a_2,\dots ,a_m$ (rows).
  2. List the elements of $B$ \in a chosen order $b_1,b_2,\dots ,b_n$ (columns).
  3. Place a $1$ \in the cell $(i,j)$ if $(a_i,b_j)\in R$; otherwise place $0$.

Edge cases:

  • Empty relation: $R=\emptyset$ gives a matrix of all $0$'s and a digraph with no edges.
  • Relation \not a function: A single element of $A$ may be related \to more than one element of $B$; the corresponding row of $M_R$ will contain more than one $1$.
  • Self‑loop: If $(a,a)\in R$, the matrix has a $1$ on the diagonal and the digraph shows a loop at vertex $a$.

Example:

Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{a,b,c\}$. Define
$$R=\{(1,a),\;(2,b),\;(2,c),\;(3,a)\}.$$

Ordered‑pair form is already given.

Matrix representation (order $A$ as $1,2,3$ and $B$ as $a,b,c$):

$a$$b$$c$
$1$$1$$0$$0$
$2$$0$$1$$1$
$3$$1$$0$$0$

Digraph:

Vertices: $1,2,3,a,b,c$. Draw arrows $1\rightarrow a$, $2\rightarrow b$, $2\rightarrow c$, $3\rightarrow a$.

Theorem (Uniqueness of matrix representation): Once the orderings of $A$ and $B$ are fixed, the Boolean matrix $M_R$ uniquely determines the relation $R$, and conversely $R$ uniquely determines $M_R$.

This systematic representation helps in analysing properties such as reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity, and is essential for further topics like functions, equivalence relations, and graph theory in the CBSE Class 12 syllabus.
long_notes.Operations on Relations (inverse, compos:
Definition of Inverse Relation: For two sets $A$ and $B$, if $R\subseteq A\times B$, the inverse of $R$, denoted $R^{-1}$, is defined as $R^{-1}=\\{(b,a)\\mid (a,b)\\in R\\}$. It swaps the order of each ordered pair.

Key Properties:

  • $(R^{-1})^{-1}=R$.
  • If $R\subseteq A\times B$ and $S\subseteq B\times C$, then $(R\circ S)^{-1}=S^{-1}\circ R^{-1}$.

Composition of Relations: Given $R\subseteq A\times B$ and $S\subseteq B\times C$, the composition $S\circ R$ is a relation from $A$ to $C$ defined by
$S\circ R=\\{(a,c)\\mid \exists b\in B\; (a,b)\\in R \text{ and } (b,c)\\in S\\}$.

Properties of Composition:

  • Associativity: $(T\circ S)\circ R = T\circ (S\circ R)$ whenever the three compositions are defined.
  • Non‑commutativity: In general $S\circ R \neq R\circ S$.

Powers of a Relation: For a relation $R$ on a set $A$, the $n^{\text{th}}$ power $R^{n}$ is defined recursively as:

  • $R^{1}=R$.
  • $R^{n+1}=R\circ R^{n}$ for $n\ge 1$.

Thus $R^{2}=R\circ R$, $R^{3}=R\circ R\circ R$, etc. $R^{0}$ is defined as the identity relation $I_{A}=\\{(a,a)\\mid a\in A\\}$.

Edge Cases:

  • If $R=\varnothing$, then $R^{-1}=\varnothing$, $R\circ S=\varnothing$, and $R^{n}=\varnothing$ for all $n\ge 1$.
  • If $R$ is not a function (i.e., some $a\in A$ relates to multiple $b$), the inverse $R^{-1}$ may fail to be a function.
  • When $R$ is not reflexive, $R^{0}$ still exists as the identity, but $R^{n}$ may never become reflexive.

Solved Example:

Let $A=\\{1,2\\}$, $B=\\{a,b\\}$, $C=\\{x,y\\}$. Define
$R=\\{(1,a),(2,b)\\}\subseteq A\times B$,
$S=\\{(a,x),(b,y)\\}\subseteq B\times C$.

1. Inverse of $R$: $R^{-1}=\\{(a,1),(b,2)\\}$.

2. Composition $S\circ R$:
We look for $b\in B$ such that $(1,b)\in R$ and $(b,c)\in S$. For $1$, $b=a$ and $(a,x)\in S$, giving $(1,x)$. For $2$, $b=b$ and $(b,y)\in S$, giving $(2,y)$. Hence $S\circ R=\\{(1,x),(2,y)\\}$.

3. Inverse of the composition: $(S\circ R)^{-1}=\\{(x,1),(y,2)\\}$, which also equals $R^{-1}\circ S^{-1}$ because $R^{-1}=\\{(a,1),(b,2)\\}$ and $S^{-1}=\\{(x,a),(y,b)\\}$, and $R^{-1}\circ S^{-1}=\\{(x,1),(y,2)\\}$ confirming the property.

4. Power $R^{2}$: $R^{2}=R\circ R$ is not defined because the codomain of the first $R$ is $B$, not $A$. However, $R^{2}$ as a relation on $A$ would be $\varnothing$.

These operations are fundamental in discrete mathematics, computer science (state transitions), and algebraic structures studied in CBSE Class 12.
long_notes.Equivalence Relations and Partially Orde:
Equivalence Relation – A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is called an equivalence relation if it satisfies:

  • Reflexive: $\forall a\in A,\; aRa$
  • Symmetric: $\forall a,b\in A,\; aRb\Rightarrow bRa$
  • Transitive: $\forall a,b,c\in A,\; aRb\land bRc\Rightarrow aRc$

When $R$ is an equivalence relation, the subset $[a]=\{x\in A\mid xRa\}$ is called the equivalence class of $a$. The collection of all distinct equivalence classes forms a partition of $A$.

Partially Ordered Relation (Poset) – A relation $R$ on $A$ is a partial order if it is:

  • Reflexive: $\forall a\in A,\; aRa$
  • Antisymmetric: $\forall a,b\in A,\; aRb\land bRa\Rightarrow a=b$
  • Transitive: $\forall a,b,c\in A,\; aRb\land bRc\Rightarrow aRc$

The ordered pair $(A,R)$ is called a partially ordered set or poset. If every pair of distinct elements is comparable, the poset is a total order.

PropertyEquivalence RelationPartial Order
Reflexive$\checkmark$$\checkmark$
Symmetric$\checkmark$$\times$
Antisymmetric$\times$$\checkmark$
Transitive$\checkmark$$\checkmark$

Edge Cases

  • Empty set: The empty relation on $\emptyset$ vacuously satisfies all four properties, thus it is both an equivalence relation and a partial order.
  • Universal relation: $R=A\times A$ is reflexive and symmetric but fails antisymmetry unless $|A|=1$, so it is not a partial order for $|A|>1$.

Solved Example (Equivalence)

Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and define $aRb\iff a\equiv b\pmod{2}$. Verify the three properties:

  • Reflexive: $a\equiv a\pmod{2}$ holds for every $a\in A$.
  • Symmetric: If $a\equiv b\pmod{2}$ then $b\equiv a\pmod{2}$.
  • Transitive: If $a\equiv b\pmod{2}$ and $b\equiv c\pmod{2}$, then $a\equiv c\pmod{2}$.

Thus $R$ is an equivalence relation. The equivalence classes are

$$[1]=\{1,3\},\qquad [2]=\{2,4\}.$$

These two classes partition $A$.

Solved Example (Partial Order)

On $B=\{1,2,3,6\}$ define $aRb\iff a\mid b$ (divides). Check:

  • Reflexive: $a\mid a$.
  • Antisymmetric: If $a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$, then $a=b$.
  • Transitive: If $a\mid b$ and $b\mid c$, then $a\mid c$.

Hence $(B,R)$ is a poset. Its Hasse diagram has $1$ at the bottom, $2$ and $3$ above it, and $6$ at the top, illustrating comparability.

These concepts are fundamental for later chapters such as Functions and Relations in the CBSE Class 12 syllabus.
long_notes.Definition of Function, Domain, Co-domai:
Definition of a Function

A relation $R$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is called a function if for every $x\in A$ there exists a unique $y\in B$ such that $(x,y)\in R$. The set $A$ is called the domain, the set $B$ the codomain, and the set of all $y$ obtained is the range.

Step‑by‑Step Derivation

  • Choose an arbitrary $x\in A$.
  • By definition of a function, there is exactly one $y\in B$ with $(x,y)\in R$.
  • Thus the mapping $x\mapsto y$ is well‑defined and single‑valued.

Hence a function can be represented as a mapping $f:A\to B$ with $f(x)=y$.

Key Laws & Theorems

  • Composition: If $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ defined by $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$.
  • Inverse (when bijective): If $f$ is one‑to‑one and onto, then $f^{-1}:B\to A$ satisfies $f^{-1}(f(x))=x$ and $f(f^{-1}(y))=y$.
  • Range Inclusion: $\operatorname{Im}(f)\subseteq B$; equality holds iff $f$ is onto.

Edge Cases

  • Constant Function: $f(x)=c$ for all $x\in A$; range is the singleton $\{c\}$.
  • Identity Function: $f(x)=x$ on $A$; domain, codomain and range all equal $A$.
  • Partial Function: Domain is a proper subset of $A$; still a function but not total.

Physical Units (SI)

When a function models a physical quantity, the codomain must carry the appropriate SI unit. For example, $f(t)=\frac{1}{2}gt^2$ (displacement in meters) maps time in seconds to distance in meters; the range inherits the meter unit.

Worked Example

Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=x^2$. The domain is $\mathbb{R}$, the codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, and the range is $[0,\infty)$. A table of values:

$x$$f(x)$
$-3$$9$
$-1$$1$
$0$$0$
$2$$4$
$5$$25$

Since $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=\pm x_2$, the function is not one‑to‑one but is onto $[0,\infty)$. Thus $f$ is a valid function with the stated domain, codomain, and range.
